analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination against LGBTQ people and women in jobs, housing, credit, and public places.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Equality Act 236-173, but the Senate never brought it to a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity into federal civil rights law, covering employment, housing, credit, public accommodations like stores and restaurants, education, and jury selection. It also strengthens protections for women, including against pregnancy discrimination. It stops the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being used as a defense against these rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender people, and women, who could sue or file federal complaints if they are fired, denied housing, denied a loan, or refused service because of who they are. This matters most in the many states with no state-level law covering these situations, including protections for transgender people using restrooms and locker rooms matching their gender identity.
analysis.who_benefits_short: LGBTQ people and women facing discrimination

how_it_helps.text: Adds sexual orientation and gender identity to the protected categories in the core federal civil rights, fair housing, equal credit, and employment discrimination laws.

Expands the definition of public accommodations to cover online retailers, health care providers, shelters, transportation services, and other businesses that provide goods and services, closing gaps in the 1964 law.
Bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 from being used as a claim or defense against these nondiscrimination protections.

Guarantees access to restrooms, locker rooms, and dressing rooms consistent with a person's gender identity, and covers discrimination based on association with an LGBTQ person or an inaccurate perception that someone is LGBTQ.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and employers, who face new compliance obligations and litigation exposure; religiously affiliated schools, adoption and foster care agencies, and other faith-based service providers, who lose the ability to raise religious-freedom objections to these nondiscrimination rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense under these titles, which religious organizations and their allies argued would force faith-based child welfare agencies, schools, and shelters to act against their beliefs or exit those services.

The expansion of public accommodations to any establishment providing a good, service, or program, including online retailers and service providers, sweeps many businesses into federal antidiscrimination liability for the first time.
A Republican motion to recommit, which would have added language stating the bill does not diminish Title IX protections, failed along nearly perfect party lines, 181-228.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people covered, the benefit is concrete: a federal right to sue when they are fired, evicted, denied credit, or refused service, which millions currently lack in states without their own protections. The costs fall on businesses and faith-based providers, and the honest trade-off is the elimination of religious-freedom defenses that courts had recognized under the 1993 Religious Freedom Restoration Act. How much weight to give that cost is the core of the dispute; the bill chose a blanket rule rather than a compromise carve-out, which is why it passed on mostly party lines.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in May 2019, but the Senate sent it to the Judiciary Committee, where it stayed without a vote until that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 13, 2019, with 240 cosponsors including 237 House Democrats and 3 House Republicans.
The House Judiciary Committee held hearings, amended the bill, and reported it by a 22-10 vote in May 2019.

On May 17, 2019, a Republican motion to recommit, which would have added language protecting Title IX, failed 181-228, and the bill passed the House 236-173, with 228 of 235 voting Democrats in favor and 8 of 197 voting Republicans in favor.
The Senate received the bill on May 20, 2019, and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, where no further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the bill, chiefly Senate Republicans who never scheduled a vote and the religious organizations that opposed it, kept the nationwide federal protections from taking effect, leaving a patchwork of state laws in place. Businesses continue to navigate varying state rules rather than one federal standard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents in the Senate and religious-exemption advocates

for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor under a rule and passed it on May 17, 2019.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the House-passed Equality Act up for a Senate vote during the 116th Congress.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 20, 2019, and took no further action on it.

against.name: 173 of 197 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 173 nay.

against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add language that nothing in the act diminishes Title IX protections; the motion failed 181-228.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was almost entirely by party: 228 of 235 voting Democrats supported it while only 8 of 197 voting Republicans did, and the committee vote was 22-10.

industries.industry: Faith-based service providers (adoption and foster agencies, religious schools, shelters)
industries.note: The bill strips the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a claim or defense against these nondiscrimination titles, closing the main legal shield such agencies had used to decline service to same-sex couples or transgender clients. Their interest in keeping that shield runs directly against the bill's protections for LGBTQ people seeking services.

Employers nationwide, not just in states with their own laws, become subject to discrimination claims based on sexual orientation and gender identity under Title VII, with new compliance and litigation exposure. Many large employers already maintain these policies voluntarily.

industries.industry: Businesses newly covered as public accommodations (online retailers, health care providers, transportation services)
industries.note: The bill expands the 1964 definition of public accommodations to any establishment providing a good, service, or program, including online retailers and health care, bringing many businesses under federal antidiscrimination rules for the first time. Businesses resisting service obligations run against the customers the bill protects.
